summaries.example: Imagine a doctor trying to help someone who is sick. The doctor watches carefully, notices signs, and tests what happens. Sanches thought this kind of careful experience was more useful than simply repeating an old rule. He also questioned whether a bright comet could decide that a king would die, because people can choose what they do.
summaries.summary: Francisco Sanches was a sixteenth- and seventeenth-century thinker who worked as a physician, medical professor, and philosopher. His best-known book is called That Nothing is Known. The title sounds as if he believed that people know absolutely nothing, but the source explains that his position was more careful. He challenged the idea that people could gain perfect knowledge by using definitions, syllogisms, and appeals to respected authorities. A syllogism is a chain of statements used to reach a conclusion. Sanches worried that such chains could merely repeat assumptions instead of proving something about the world. He preferred starting with particular things that could be observed, while admitting that the senses show us appearances rather than the deepest nature of things. His medical training helped shape this approach: doctors must pay attention to what they can see and experience when diagnosing and treating illness. In his poem about the comet of 1577, he rejected the belief that comets predict disasters or control human actions. He argued that human choices depend on free will, not on distant stars. In a letter to the mathematician Christopher Clavius, Sanches also questioned the idea that mathematical truths are completely certain and independent of experience. Later writers noticed similarities between Sanches's questioning style and Descartes's method of doubt, although the two philosophers reached different conclusions. Sanches's doubt was constructive: he ended by urging people to keep working, examining things, and asking questions.
key_ideas: Francisco Sanches was both a physician and a philosopher who questioned claims of perfect knowledge.
He trusted careful observation more than famous authorities or complicated word games.
He argued that comets do not prove that bad events will happen or control human choices.
His doubt was meant to encourage more investigation, not to make people stop learning.
His ideas were later discussed in connection with René Descartes and the history of modern philosophy.
summaries.why_it_matters: Sanches shows that questioning is not the same as giving up. Careful doubt can help people notice weak reasons, test claims, and avoid being fooled by impressive language. His work also connects philosophy with medicine, science, language, and the study of free choice. Learning about him helps us see that important ideas often develop through arguments among several thinkers, not from one person working alone.

summaries.example: Suppose a medical student is told that a symptom always proves one particular disease. A Sanches-style response would ask: What observations support that connection? Has it been tested in particular cases? Does the diagnosis explain the patient, or does it merely repeat a definition? This does not require refusing all treatment. It means using experience and reason while recognizing that observation may reveal appearances without giving perfect knowledge of an underlying nature.
summaries.summary: Francisco Sanches was an Iberian physician, professor of medicine and philosophy, and a major figure in the history of early modern skepticism. His principal philosophical work, Quod nihil scitur, usually translated as That Nothing is Known, attacks the scholastic aspiration to demonstrative and perfectly certain knowledge. Sanches's title should not be read as a simple claim that no cognition of any kind is possible. Rather, he argues that the traditional account of science fails to establish the kind of complete understanding it promises. Definitions cannot simply be assumed to disclose essences, and syllogisms cannot generate more certainty than their premises possess. If primary principles are indemonstrable inventions accepted by faith, conclusions derived from them are only as secure as those assumptions. Sanches is therefore suspicious of metaphysical entities and universals that cannot be connected to natural phenomena or particular objects of perception. His nominalist tendency treats general terms as linguistically useful but insufficient to reveal the natures of things. Sense perception is necessary, yet it is also limited: it presents outward qualities, and the mind works with images supplied by the senses. Even accurate observation does not thereby provide access to a thing's essence, origin, or causes. His medical background helps explain why this skepticism remains practical. Diagnosis requires observation of particular cases and attention to what appears, not confidence in abstract verbal systems alone. In his poem on the comet of 1577, Sanches rejects astrological predictions that comets announce plague, death, or political disaster. He also denies that celestial bodies determine voluntary action. key_ideas: Sanches's central target is the claim that Aristotelian scholastic methods yield perfect knowledge simply through authoritative definitions and demonstrations.
His empiricist skepticism begins with particular, perceptible things, but he argues that perception gives access mainly to appearances or qualities, not essences or things in themselves.
He treats definitions and first principles as insufficiently secure when they are accepted without demonstration; conclusions drawn from them may therefore inherit their uncertainty.
His criticism of astrology and comet prophecy combines skepticism about causal inference with a defense of human freedom.
In the letter to Christopher Clavius, he opposes a strongly Platonist conception of mathematics and emphasizes geometrical measurement and sensible objects.
Sanches's relation to Academic and Pyrrhonian skepticism is debated in the source, but his skepticism is presented as mitigated and practically oriented rather than simply destructive.
summaries.why_it_matters: Sanches matters because he illustrates a form of skepticism that can function as intellectual discipline. By challenging authority, circular definitions, and unsupported causal claims, he asks how inquiry can remain connected to evidence. His work also helps explain a transition in philosophy from inherited metaphysical systems toward questions about knowledge, method, language, and perception. The view that knowledge begins from sense experience and observation rather than from purely innate or abstract principles.

summaries.example: Suppose someone says, “Whenever a red sunset appears, tomorrow’s game will be canceled.” You could ask whether the sunset has ever been shown to cause cancellations, whether many sunsets occur before games that continue normally, and whether the claim is based on observation or just a story. Sanches used a similar attitude toward claims that comets predicted disasters. He also thought people’s choices could not be controlled by a star.
summaries.summary: Francisco Sanches was a physician, medical professor, and philosopher who lived from 1551 to 1623. He became known for a book whose title is usually translated as That Nothing is Known. Sanches was a skeptic, meaning that he carefully questioned whether people had really proved what they claimed to know. His target was especially the scholastic use of Aristotle: school thinkers often relied on authoritative texts, technical definitions, and syllogisms. Sanches argued that a chain of reasoning cannot create perfect knowledge if its first assumptions have not themselves been established. A definition may appear to explain a word while only using other unclear words. In this way, language can create the appearance of understanding without showing the nature of a real thing. Sanches also favored an empiricist approach. He thought inquiry should begin with particular things available to observation, not with invisible universals or abstract entities treated as unquestionably real. Yet he did not believe the senses solved every problem. Senses reveal how things appear, and the mind works with those appearances; they do not necessarily reveal a thing’s essence or deepest cause. His medical training made this limitation important but useful. A doctor has to observe bodies, symptoms, and results, even if medicine cannot explain every underlying nature with perfect certainty. Sanches applied similar criticism to astrology. In his poem about the comet of 1577, he argued that a comet could not reliably foretell plague, deaths, harvest failures, or other events. Nor could it determine a person’s voluntary actions, since that would undermine free will. key_ideas: Sanches questioned the school tradition that relied heavily on Aristotle, commentaries, authority, and formal demonstrations.
He argued that complicated reasoning cannot prove more than the starting assumptions allow.
He believed we encounter particular objects through the senses, while general terms may not reveal what things truly are.
His medical work encouraged attention to observation and practical results.
He rejected the idea that comets predict disasters or control human decisions.
His skepticism was active: it pushed people to investigate rather than simply accept or reject everything.
summaries.why_it_matters: Sanches matters because he connects skepticism with practical inquiry. He shows why students should distinguish between a conclusion that follows from an argument and a conclusion that has been supported by reliable evidence. His work also helps explain why later philosophers became increasingly interested in knowledge, method, perception, and language. Comparing him with Descartes reveals that two thinkers can begin with doubt but use it for different purposes: Sanches emphasizes observation and limited, useful knowledge, while Descartes seeks a firmer foundation in reason.
